messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: transform cauchy prior
parts:
As indicated from previous posts, if X ~ uniform(-pi/2, pi/2), tan(X) ~ cauchy(0, 1).  So a trick is suggested to replace cauchy prior with uniform.  I am sure this transform would help if we just want to draw from cauchy distribution.  But when it is a prior, it seems it would not improve necessarily.

In the logistic regression model posted a couple days ago, using this trick would not improve the effective sample size.  I also look at smaller examples such as the following
 two, where there is no much difference for the effective sample sizes.  In detail, I simulated 1000 sets of data, estimated using these two models and looked the n_eff for sigma. 

> summary(neffs_m1)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1102    1692    1812    1803    1920    2303 
> summary(neffs_m2)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1088    1542    1648    1644    1753    2060 


//// model 1 

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  mu ~ cauchy(0, 10);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}  

//// model 2
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=-pi()/2, upper=pi()/2> mu_unif;
  real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> sigma_unif;
}
transformed parameters {
  real mu;
  real sigma;
  mu <- tan(mu_unif);
  sigma <- tan(sigma_unif);
}
model {
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
} 


Jiqiang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] transform cauchy prior
parts:
Thanks for reporting back on this -- understanding
these issues is super-critical for efficient
sampling (though in this case it appears to
not make much of a difference!).

How big was N and what were the simulation
values for mu and sigma?

The second model isn't quite the same in
that it produces an implicit Cauchy(0,1)
prior on mu and half Cauchy(0,1) on sigma. I
don't even have a sense of whether a more constrained
prior will speed up or slow down sampling or neither.

I'd love to see what the geometry looks like
in terms of log probability versus parameters,
(mu,sigma) in model1 and (mu_unif,sigma_unif) in
model2. I'd also be curious about just transforming
one of the params, so that'd be a model 3 with (mu_unif,sigma)
and model 4 with (mu,sigma_unif). I just don't have
a good sense of what these look like.

I also wonder how it would compare to transforming
a normal(0,1) rather than a uniform, but I suspect
it'd be similar to the implied logistic you get with
a uniform in Stan. The code would look like:

sigma_norm ~ normal(0,1);
...
sigma <- tan(pi() * (Phi(sigma_norm) - 0.5)); // sigma ~ cauchy(0,1);

I like the idea of constraining sigma_unif to
(0, pi/2). It's super convenient.

Were the times the same? What we really care
about is n_eff/second, not n_eff/iteration.

I like the logistic regression test case because
that's one's not only realistic, it's a model we
care about.

The second model, having transformed params, does
a bit more writing, but I doubt it's a bottleneck.
A timed test with mu and sigma local variables would
be a more minimal test of the actual transform's speed.

- Bob

With this R code:

library(rstan)

y <- rnorm(1000)

model_code <-
'

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
}
parameters {

real mu_raw;
  real<lower=0> sigma_raw;

}
transformed parameters {
  real mu;
  real sigma;

mu <- 10 * tan(pi() * (Phi(mu_raw) - 0.5));
  sigma <- 5 * tan(pi() * (Phi(sigma_raw) - 0.5));
}
model {
  mu_raw ~ normal(0,1);
  sigma_raw ~ normal(0,1);
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}
'

library(rstan)
m1 <- '

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
} 
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

mu ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}
'

m2 <- '

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
} 
parameters {

real<lower=0, upper=pi()/2> sigma_unif;
  real<lower=-pi()/2, upper=pi()/2> mu_unif;
}

transformed parameters {
  real sigma;
  real mu;
  sigma <- 5 * tan(sigma_unif);  
  mu <- 5 * tan(mu_unif);

}
model { 
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

'

m3 <- '

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real y[N];
} 
parameters {

real sigma_norm;
  real mu_norm;
}

transformed parameters {
  real sigma;
  real mu;
  sigma <- 5 * tan(pi() * Phi(sigma_norm) * 0.5);
  mu <- 5 * tan(pi() * (Phi(sigma_norm) - 0.5));

}
model { 
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

'


fit1 <- stan(model_code = m1);
fit2 <- stan(model_code = m2);
fit3 <- stan(model_code = m3);

fun1 <- function(y) {
  t <- system.time(fit <- stan(fit = fit1, data = list(N = length(y), y = y), refresh = -1)) 
  c(summary(fit)$summary[c('mu', 'sigma'), 'n_eff'], t)
} 

fun2 <- function(y) {
  t <- system.time(fit <- stan(fit = fit2, data = list(N = length(y), y = y), refresh = -1)) 
  c(summary(fit)$summary[c('mu', 'sigma'), 'n_eff'], t)
} 

fun3 <- function(y) {
  t <- system.time(fit <- stan(fit = fit3, data = list(N = length(y), y = y), refresh = -1)) 
  c(summary(fit)$summary[c('mu', 'sigma'), 'n_eff'], t)
} 

N <- 30
ys <- lapply(1:200, FUN = function(i) rnorm(N)) 
s1 <- lapply(ys, FUN = fun1) 
s2 <- lapply(ys, FUN = fun2) 
s3 <- lapply(ys, FUN = fun3) 

s1 <- do.call(rbind, s1)
s2 <- do.call(rbind, s2)
s3 <- do.call(rbind, s3)

I think we should have a really, really high threshold before we make a function name change meaning. Maybe at some point we could have Phi_precise() and Phi_approx() and make references to Phi() return an error message that says "Did you mean Phi_precise() or Phi_approx()?" That said, any difference in the results between the two will presumably be less than the simulation noise. But for optimization, it is of some value to be able to replicate R or whatever program that utilizes the standard normal CDF "exactly".

Ben

I also added a custom gradient implementation, which will make

Even better. Now that we have Phi_approx(), we should press to make the following variant of the Matt trick be a thing in Stan:

-- let z have a standard normal prior
-- let p = Phi_approx(z) be a quantile
-- let theta = Q(p) be a parameter where Q(p) is some quantile function

For Columbia people, the best reference for utilizing quantile functions is

http://dx.doi.org.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/10.1201/9781420035919

particularly chapters 5 -- 7. I had mentioned the generalized lambda distribution(s) --- which is / are defined by its / their quantile function(s) --- can approximate any continuous unimodal distribution, which are covered in chapter 7. Doing something like this for data would require more work because you often have to solve for the root of an implicit function to get the p.  But for priors on parameters, users could implement it pretty easily in their .stan files.

Ben

We can replace these two steps by declaring z to be
a constrained variable between 0 and 1. That way, we
wind up using the even more efficient logistic transform.

I don't know how the difference between the implied logistic
distribution in our uniforms and doing this transform would
affect the geometry. If it's a huge help, we could change
the way we do bounded scalar transforms under the hood.
